demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The event happened because of the way I acted
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the trigger set is clinically incoherent. All three triggers are positively valenced interpersonal cues (affection, praise, positive emotion) with no trauma-specific or guilt-linked cue; as a trio they are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with this trauma type, where reminders of responsibility, injury, driving/scene cues, or criticism are more plausible. While one such item could occur idiosyncratically, all three together are implausible.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I am permanently an outsider now' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile and trauma type. The other appraisals center on guilt and diminished capability, which fit accidental injury, but a stable outsider/alienation identity is not well supported by the selected triggers or memory items and is more characteristic of chronic interpersonal trauma or stigmatized victimization. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a coherent guilt-based formulation.

vignette:
Priya is a 31-year-old South Asian woman who works as a third-grade teacher at an elementary school in the suburbs of Atlanta. She is married, and by most outward measures her life before the accident had been quietly purposeful - she was the kind of teacher parents requested by name, the kind who stayed late laminating things and arrived early to rearrange the reading corner. That version of herself feels, to Priya, like someone she is no longer permitted to be.

Fourteen months ago, Priya was driving home from a school supply run on a Saturday afternoon, her back seat loaded with construction paper and paint sets. At an intersection she knew well, she misjudged the gap in oncoming traffic while making a left turn. The collision that followed was not catastrophic by statistical measures, but it was catastrophic to her: the driver she struck, a man in his fifties, sustained a fractured pelvis and a serious head injury that required weeks of hospitalisation. In the immediate aftermath, Priya sat on the pavement with the smell of engine fluid and something sweetly chemical - later she would identify it as the paint sets that had burst open - filling the air around her. She remembers the event not as a continuous sequence but as a series of frozen images: the other car's grille filling her windshield, her own hands on the steering wheel, a paramedic's fluorescent vest, the man's face through a car window before she looked away. These pictures have never softened into narrative distance. When they surface, they do not feel like memories of something that happened over a year ago - they feel like something happening now, accompanied by that same sharp chemical smell, her body responding as though she is still sitting on that pavement.

In the months that followed, Priya came to believe, with the force of settled conviction, that the accident happened because of something essential and defective in her - not a lapse in judgment but a revelation of who she actually was. She had always been praised for her competence, her care, her reliability. The accident reframed all of it as illusion. She was certain she was no longer capable of the things that had defined her, and she had begun to feel that the accident had placed her permanently outside the ordinary human community - that other people moved through their lives with a coherence she had forfeited. These appraisals did not stay abstract. They reached directly into her memory, pulling the frozen images forward with renewed intensity whenever she found herself thinking about what she had done. The belief that she was to blame made it impossible to let the memory recede; returning to it felt, paradoxically, like the only honest thing she could do.

The appraisals also shaped what became unbearable to encounter. Because she had come to understand herself as fundamentally incapable and fraudulent, praise felt like an accusation. When a parent emailed to say Priya had transformed their child's relationship with reading, she found herself back on that pavement within seconds - the smell, the frozen images, the present-tense terror. Positive emotions carried the same charge: a moment of genuine warmth in the classroom would tip without warning into the sensory and visual texture of the accident, as though happiness itself was something she had lost the right to. Any conversation among colleagues about road accidents - not uncommon in a school staffroom - functioned as an immediate portal. The memory, once triggered, would then intensify the triggers themselves: having been flooded by the images once in response to praise, she became hypervigilant to it, scanning for compliments the way someone scans for a threat.

Over the course of the school year, Priya began deflecting praise with a reflexive brevity that her colleagues read as modesty. She stopped joining staffroom conversations and began eating lunch alone in her classroom. She had not told her husband the full weight of what she carries, in part because she was afraid that articulating it would confirm it.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when a student ran up to hug her and she stood rigid, unable to respond, smelling paint. She is most afraid that she will never be the teacher - or the person - she was before. She is hoping, with considerable ambivalence, to be told that is not true.
